doc.title: Frank Capp interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

chapter: Opinions on Jazz and Big Band Life
title: Jazz education then and now
summary: Capp says there was no jazz education when he was in school, and praises school programs producing young players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well what’s happened, thanks to our education system, they have allowed, or have created jazz programs. When I was in school, you couldn’t even use the word jazz. That was a no-no. There was no jazz education at all. In my high school, all I got was a music appreciation class and we listened to classics. Nothing. Jazz was an illegitimate music as far as that era of thinking was concerned. But certainly we know better than that now and certainly because of the great educational program, there is all kinds of young kids coming up. And you say, jeez, where’d they learn how to do that? Well they learned how to do it in school. All they need is a little experience and to sand off some of the rough edges and they’ll be great. They’ll be equally as good as any of us who so-called grew up with that music you know.
Yeah. I think Herb Ellis said some of them just need to figure out what not to play now.
That’s right. Exactly, exactly. But music is, all music is great, except one.
